title: Tesla Weighs China Business Sale to Clear Path for SpaceX Merger
excerpt: The Wall Street Journal reports that Tesla executives have been told to prepare for a separation of the company's Chinese operations ahead of a potential merger with SpaceX, though Elon Musk has called the report "absurdly fake news."
body:
• Tesla advisers have discussed options for separating its China business, including a spinoff, sale, or closure, ahead of a potential SpaceX merger, according to the Wall Street Journal.
  • Elon Musk denied the report on X, calling it "absurdly fake news" and saying the topic "has never even been brought up in any conversation."
  • Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory is its largest plant globally, with capacity exceeding 950,000 vehicles and accounting for over half of the company's global deliveries.
  • A SpaceX-Tesla merger would face intense regulatory scrutiny, particularly from Beijing, given SpaceX's role as a major U.S. defense contractor with access to classified programs.

Tesla executives have been told to prepare for a separation of the company's China business ahead of a potential merger with SpaceX, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the talks.

Tesla advisers have discussed possible options for the separation, including a spinoff, sale, or outright closure of the Chinese operations, according to another person cited by the Journal. It remains unclear how quickly Tesla could execute such a move, and the plans could still change.

"Obviously we can't talk about, you know, combining companies and that kind of thing on earnings calls. It is got to be done with the appropriate process."

— Elon Musk, on Tesla's earnings call last week

Musk responded to the report on X, the social media platform he owns, calling it "absurdly fake news" and adding: "This has never even been brought up in any conversation."

Why China Is the Sticking Point

A merger between Tesla and SpaceX would raise significant geopolitical and regulatory hurdles, particularly involving China. SpaceX is a major U.S. defense contractor involved in national security and classified satellite programs. Sales to the U.S. government accounted for 20.9% of SpaceX's business in 2025, according to the Journal.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=3srUKWyp1Pw

Beijing would likely subject a merger to intense scrutiny, given concerns that a U.S. defense contractor would gain control of Tesla's Chinese factories, supply chain know-how, and data from roughly two million Tesla owners in China, according to people familiar with the matter. China would probably demand guardrails to prevent SpaceX's influence from reaching Tesla's Chinese subsidiary and to block the transfer of dual-use goods such as rare-earth materials.

Tesla's Gigafactory Shanghai, which began production in October 2019 as China's first wholly foreign-owned car plant, is the company's largest and most productive facility globally. It produces the Model 3 and Model Y, has annual capacity exceeding 950,000 vehicles, and accounted for more than half of Tesla's global deliveries in 2025, according to Tesla vice president Grace Tao. The factory serves as Tesla's primary export hub for Europe, Canada, and the Asia-Pacific region.

Unlike many Western automakers operating in China, Tesla runs its operations independently without a local joint-venture partner. China was Tesla's second-largest market after the U.S., generating $4.7 billion in revenue in the April-to-June quarter — roughly 17% of the company's total $28 billion in quarterly revenue.

Musk's Long-Running Contingency Planning

The separation discussions are not entirely new. Musk had in recent years instructed Tesla executives to organize the company with a "laser" between its U.S. and China businesses, the Journal reported, citing sources. The goal was to ensure that in the event of geopolitical strife between Washington and Beijing, at least the U.S. half of Tesla would survive.

Musk was particularly concerned about Tesla's dependence on China for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells and feared its semiconductor access could be jeopardized if Beijing moved against Taiwan, where TSMC — the world's largest contract chip maker — is based. The contingency planning targeted readiness by 2026 or 2027.

During the first Trump administration, Tesla launched an initiative called "Project Carbon" to relocate its Chinese suppliers to Mexico. By 2025, Tesla decided to stop using China-based suppliers entirely in its U.S. factories by 2027, driven partly by U.S. tariffs and government incentives for domestic production.

SpaceX IPO Intensifies Merger Talk

Speculation about a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination has intensified following SpaceX's record-setting initial public offering in June, which raised $86 billion for the company. Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, has recently talked up the crossover potential between the two firms as he reorganizes them around artificial intelligence projects.

Executives have also discussed creating a separate sales entity to handle exports from Tesla's Shanghai plant and establishing isolated office systems that would bar China-based employees from direct access to other company units, according to the Journal. Currently, Tesla China has some autonomy, but employees largely work together globally, and the top executive in China, Tom Zhu, oversees all of Tesla's global automotive business.

Precedents and What's Next

Cross-border mergers involving China have a complicated track record. In 2018, Qualcomm abandoned its proposed acquisition of Dutch chip maker NXP Semiconductors after failing to secure Chinese regulatory clearance. Several U.S. companies have preemptively separated their China units: Starbucks recently sold a majority stake in its China business, and Yum Brands spun off its China arm in 2016, selling stakes to local investors.

Tesla sources more than 95% of components for its China-made vehicles from over 400 domestic Chinese suppliers, with more than 60 of those also serving Tesla's global operations. Any separation would need to untangle this deeply localized supply chain while maintaining production continuity — a challenge that could take years to execute. With merger talk accelerating and geopolitical tensions showing no signs of easing, the future of Tesla's most productive factory hangs in the balance.
